name: Marley Marl
hook: Made a mistake in a mixing session, caught a snare drum off a record by accident, and worked out on the spot that this was better than any drum machine.
blurb: In 1984, working on someone else's record, Marlon Williams was trying to grab a piece of a vocal and accidentally caught the snare drum along with it. He noticed it sounded better than the snare on his drum machine, and understood immediately what that meant: you could take the drums off any record ever made and build a new beat out of them. That is the technique almost all hip-hop production rests on, and it started as a mistake. It is the hinge between the drum machine era and the sampling era. The 808 and the 909 made their drum sounds electronically. Sampling gave you the real sound of one drummer in one room, with the tape, the compression and the other instruments bleeding in already part of it. The results ran both ways: a huge expansion of the sounds producers could use, and the copyright rules that grew up around it once it became clear what had been taken and from whom. Accounts of the session name the record and the year consistently, but the sources consulted here do not name the sampler he was using, so this record does not name one.

signatureTracks.title: The Bridge (produced for MC Shan)
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: The record that started the Bridge Wars, and an early full demonstration of drums lifted off other people's records.

signatureTracks.title: The Symphony (produced for the Juice Crew)
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: Four MCs taking turns over one of his loops. The template for the posse cut, and the loop is the fixed thing everyone else works against.
